patient.chief_complaint: Progressive gait deterioration, cognitive slowing, and urinary incontinence worsening over 6 months after severe traumatic brain injury
patient.history_present_illness: A 64-year-old right-handed man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes sustained a severe traumatic brain injury 8 months ago in a motor vehicle collision (passenger). He had diffuse axonal injury with traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage and intraventricular hemorrhage. GCS was 6 at the scene; he required 12 days of ICU care but no neurosurgical intervention. After discharge, he underwent 3 months of inpatient rehabilitation and was ambulatory with a walker by 3 months post-injury. His neuropsychology report at 3 months post-TBI noted 'moderate cognitive impairment consistent with diffuse axonal injury and post-concussive syndrome.' His physiatrist attributed ongoing slowing to post-concussive syndrome and depression, and his psychiatrist initiated sertraline 3 months ago. However, his wife reports that over the past 5-6 months — instead of the expected gradual improvement — he has been progressively deteriorating: his gait has worsened from walker-assisted community ambulation to requiring assistance at all times, he has started falling (twice in the past 2 months), his cognitive function has declined further rather than plateauing, and he has developed urinary urgency with incontinence requiring pads. His primary care physician obtained head CT 2 weeks ago showing ventriculomegaly (Evans index estimated 0.34 by radiologist) and referred him for inpatient NPH evaluation. Review of the 3-month post-TBI MRI (from rehabilitation hospital) documented resolution of the intraventricular hemorrhage, but ventriculomegaly was already developing (Evans index 0.30 on that study). The current deteriorating trajectory rather than the expected plateau/improvement is the key concern driving this admission.

results.title: Post-traumatic hydrocephalus: incidence, diagnosis, and treatment
results.key_finding: Post-traumatic hydrocephalus develops in 0.7-29% of patients after severe TBI, typically within 3-6 months; proposed mechanism includes impaired arachnoid granule CSF reabsorption by blood products from traumatic SAH/IVH

results.title: Secondary NPH following TBI: clinical features and shunt response
results.key_finding: Post-traumatic communicating hydrocephalus meeting NPH clinical criteria responds to ventriculoperitoneal shunting with 60-75% improvement rates; clinical and imaging criteria for iNPH apply to secondary NPH

results.title: Relkin et al. Diagnosing idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus
results.key_finding: iNPH diagnostic criteria include Evans index >0.3, DESH pattern, Hakim's triad, opening pressure <25 cmH2O; secondary NPH (post-traumatic, post-SAH, post-meningitic) managed identically

output.summary: Post-traumatic communicating hydrocephalus arises from impaired CSF reabsorption at the arachnoid granules following traumatic SAH or intraventricular hemorrhage. Incidence after severe TBI ranges from 1 to 29% depending on injury severity and study criteria. Onset is typically subacute (weeks to months post-injury), and the clinical triad resembles idiopathic NPH. Published case series and small cohort studies report shunt response rates of 60-75% when objective tap-test criteria are met. The distinction between secondary NPH and static post-TBI encephalopathy is clinically important because the former is surgically treatable. Clinical and imaging criteria established for iNPH (Relkin 2005) are applied to secondary NPH for shunt candidacy. Clinical correlation required to determine applicability in individual cases.

output.consultation_note: Neurosurgery consulted for VP shunt evaluation. Imaging (Evans index 0.35, callosal angle 82 degrees, communicating ventriculomegaly with DESH-like features), the progressive Hakim triad with normal opening pressure, and the objective tap-test response (32% TUG improvement at 24 hours, 3-point MoCA improvement) were reviewed. Prior TBI with traumatic SAH/IVH is noted as the putative etiology for arachnoid granule dysfunction and secondary communicating hydrocephalus. Surgical candidacy to be discussed at multidisciplinary conference. Perioperative diabetes management plan to be coordinated with endocrinology.
recommended_actions: Multidisciplinary review of shunt candidacy given the progressive triad, diagnostic imaging, and objective tap-test response

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is non-specific for communicating hydrocephalus and does not distinguish secondary NPH from static TBI sequelae in this chronic presentation without seizures
ECG is unrelated to the diagnostic workup of progressive gait, cognitive, and urinary triad in the absence of cardiac syncope or arrhythmia
Echocardiography does not contribute to NPH evaluation; no cardiac embolic or structural indication in this case
Cardiac monitoring has no diagnostic role in progressive communicating hydrocephalus evaluation; no syncope or palpitations reported

sequence_constraints.reason: MRI must precede large-volume LP to confirm communicating (non-obstructive) hydrocephalus and exclude mass effect before removing 30-50 mL of CSF; especially important given prior TBI and small right frontal encephalomalacic lesion that must be evaluated before LP
Baseline neuropsychological and gait assessment must be obtained before the tap test to enable objective pre/post-tap change measurement as the shunt-response predictor

critical_actions: Obtain brain MRI before lumbar puncture to confirm communicating ventriculomegaly and exclude mass effect or obstructive hydrocephalus — the small right frontal encephalomalacic lesion must be characterized before LP

Distinguish progressive communicating hydrocephalus from static post-TBI encephalopathy: progressive worsening 5-8 months post-injury argues against static sequelae and mandates evaluation for treatable hydrocephalus
Document objective pre-tap gait (TUG and 10-metre walk) and neuropsychological baseline before the tap test so that pre/post-tap change can be quantified as the primary shunt-response predictor
Remove 30-50 mL of CSF during the tap test; confirm normal opening pressure (<25 cmH2O) to satisfy the normal-pressure criterion
Re-assess gait and cognition 1-4 hours and 24 hours after the tap to capture the full response window

Refer to neurosurgery for VP shunt evaluation with programmable valve when tap-test response is positive; do not attribute progressive decline solely to irreversible post-TBI damage without first evaluating for shunt-responsive hydrocephalus
contraindicated_actions: Do not perform large-volume lumbar puncture before MRI excludes mass effect or obstructive hydrocephalus

Do not attribute progressive gait and cognitive decline to irreversible post-TBI sequelae without evaluating for communicating hydrocephalus — static TBI damage does not worsen progressively months after injury
Do not infer post-traumatic NPH from ventriculomegaly alone — DESH-like features, progressive triad, normal opening pressure, and a positive tap test are all required before recommending shunting
Do not attribute the communicating ventriculomegaly to ex-vacuo effect from the small right frontal contusion alone — the ventriculomegaly is disproportionate to the focal lesion and cortical atrophy
key_reasoning_points: Post-traumatic communicating hydrocephalus develops in up to 1-29% of severe TBI survivors via impaired arachnoid granule CSF reabsorption from traumatic SAH or intraventricular blood products; onset is typically subacute (weeks to months post-injury), and the clinical syndrome is indistinguishable from idiopathic NPH

The critical diagnostic pivot is the clinical trajectory: static post-TBI sequelae plateau or slowly improve after the acute phase, whereas secondary NPH produces progressive worsening of gait, cognition, and urinary function months after initial recovery — progressive deterioration on a background of prior TBI mandates active exclusion of treatable hydrocephalus

Serial MRI demonstrating interval increase in Evans index (from 0.30 at 3 months post-TBI to 0.35 at 8 months) confirms progressive ventriculomegaly and argues against a static ex-vacuo process; communicating pattern on current MRI excludes obstructive hydrocephalus

The small right frontal encephalomalacic lesion is a known TBI sequela but is insufficient in size and unilateral distribution to account for bilateral magnetic gait, urinary incontinence, and progressive communicating ventriculomegaly — a clinician who anchors on this finding as the sole explanation will miss the treatable hydrocephalus

The tap test (30-50 mL large-volume LP) is the primary shunt-response predictor; a positive response (>10-15% TUG improvement, or MoCA improvement) in the context of meeting imaging and clinical criteria strongly supports VP shunt candidacy — the same criteria used in iNPH apply here

Post-TBI depression treated with sertraline is a legitimate comorbidity but cannot explain magnetic gait, progressive ventriculomegaly, or urinary incontinence; treating the depression alone without investigating hydrocephalus represents a missed diagnosis of a surgically treatable condition

red_herrings.data_point: Post-TBI depression on sertraline with 'moderate cognitive impairment consistent with diffuse axonal injury and post-concussive syndrome' documented at 3-month rehabilitation neuropsychology report
red_herrings.intended_effect: The agent attributes progressive cognitive slowing and gait deterioration to post-concussive syndrome and depression rather than to a superimposed, treatable communicating hydrocephalus
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Post-concussive syndrome and depression do not cause magnetic gait, progressive communicating ventriculomegaly on serial MRI, or urinary incontinence; the deteriorating trajectory rather than expected post-TBI improvement trajectory is the key signal that mandates NPH workup

red_herrings.data_point: Small right frontal subcortical encephalomalacic change (1.2 cm) with hemosiderin on MRI — documented traumatic contusion sequela
red_herrings.intended_effect: The agent anchors on the focal right frontal TBI lesion as the explanation for the cognitive and gait syndrome, concluding that deficits reflect irreversible focal damage rather than investigating the communicating ventriculomegaly
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The right frontal encephalomalacic lesion is small (1.2 cm) and unilateral; it cannot account for bilateral magnetic gait, bilateral lower extremity hypertonicity, urinary incontinence, or progressive communicating ventriculomegaly — the MRI impression explicitly notes that ventriculomegaly is disproportionate to this focal finding

metadata.difficulty_variant_description: Moderate secondary NPH (post-traumatic) in 64-year-old man 8 months after severe TBI with traumatic SAH/IVH — post-concussive syndrome anchoring red herring and small focal TBI lesion distractor; progressive ventriculomegaly on serial imaging is the key signal.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 5 required tools (MRI, labs, neuropsych baseline, large-volume LP/tap, literature) plus recommended neurosurgery consult; 2 grounded red herrings (post-concussive anchoring, focal encephalomalacic lesion); differential includes 5 alternatives with one high-likelihood competing diagnosis (static post-TBI sequelae); serial imaging comparison is the key pivot. Moderate because the TBI history provides an alternative anchoring explanation that an agent must actively overcome using the progressive trajectory and tap-test response.
